The word saffron has two related meanings as a noun: a spice and a color. The color meaning comes directly from the spice, so understanding the spice first makes everything click.

Saffron is the world's most expensive spice. It comes from a small flower called Crocus sativus — a purple, cup-shaped flower that blooms in autumn. Inside each flower are three tiny, thread-like strands called stigmas. These delicate, dark red threads are saffron. That's it — the entire spice is just those three little threads per flower.

Why is it so expensive?
Because it can only be harvested by hand, carefully, one flower at a time. Each flower gives only three threads. To collect just one pound (about 450 grams) of saffron, you need to pick threads from roughly 70,000 to 250,000 flowers. That is an enormous amount of human labor for a tiny quantity of spice. No machine can do this job well. The flowers also bloom for only about two weeks per year, so the entire harvest window is very short. Iran produces the vast majority of the world's saffron. Kashmir (India), Spain, and Morocco also produce notable amounts.

What do the threads look like?
Fresh saffron threads are deep crimson-red to dark orange-red at one end, with a slightly lighter or yellowish tip. They are very thin, almost hair-like, and about 2–4 cm long.

What does saffron taste and smell like?
Saffron has a unique, complex flavor and aroma that is hard to compare to anything else. It is:

  • Floral — gently fragrant, like a delicate flower
  • Slightly earthy or hay-like — with a warm, almost musky depth
  • Mildly bitter — there's a slight bitterness, but it's pleasant and not sharp
  • Faintly metallic or honey-like — many people notice a subtle sweetness with a metallic edge

This combination is what makes saffron irreplaceable in cooking. No other spice tastes quite like it.

What does saffron do in food?
Saffron does two things when added to food:

  1. It colors the food a beautiful golden-yellow. When you soak a few threads in warm water, milk, or broth, the liquid slowly turns a rich, glowing yellow-gold. This golden color is saffron's most visually dramatic quality.
  2. It adds flavor and fragrance. Even a tiny pinch — just a few threads — is enough to perfume an entire dish. Using too much can actually make food taste bitter and medicinal, so less is more.

How is it used in cooking?
Saffron is a core ingredient in many beloved dishes around the world:

  • Biryani (South Asia) — the golden color and floral fragrance of biryani comes largely from saffron
  • Paella (Spain) — the iconic golden rice dish gets its color and depth from saffron
  • Risotto alla Milanese (Italy) — a classic saffron-infused creamy rice
  • Bouillabaisse (France) — a Provençal fish stew fragrant with saffron
  • Persian rice and stews — saffron is central to Persian/Iranian cuisine
  • Kheer and sweets — saffron is used in Indian milk-based desserts and sweets like gulab jamun and rasmalai

A common technique is to first "bloom" saffron — soaking the threads in a small amount of warm (not boiling) liquid for 10–30 minutes before adding it to the dish. This releases its color and flavor much more effectively than tossing dry threads directly into a pot.

Medicinal and other uses
For thousands of years, saffron has also been used in traditional medicine — in Ayurveda, Persian medicine, and others — for things like improving mood, aiding digestion, and acting as a mild sedative. Modern research has shown genuine promise in saffron's potential to support mood and act as an antioxidant, though it is not a medicine in the clinical sense. It has also been used historically as a dye for fabric and cosmetics, producing yellow-orange hues.

As a noun, saffron also refers to a deep, warm golden-yellow color — sometimes leaning slightly orange. It is the color you see when saffron is dissolved in liquid: a rich, glowing yellow-gold, like sunshine condensed.

This color is deeply significant in several cultures:

  • In Hinduism, saffron (also called kesari in Hindi) is a sacred color representing fire, purity, and renunciation. It is the color worn by Hindu saints, monks, and ascetics, and seen on the Indian national flag.
  • In Buddhism, monks traditionally wear robes dyed in saffron or ochre (a related golden-orange), representing simplicity, humility, and detachment from the material world.

As...Saffron is...
A spiceThe dried red threads (stigmas) from the crocus flower, used for color, flavor, and fragrance in cooking
A colorA warm, rich golden-yellow, the color the spice produces in liquid

If you can only remember one thing: saffron is a precious, hand-harvested spice made of tiny red threads from a flower, famous for turning food a gorgeous golden-yellow and adding a floral, earthy, faintly sweet fragrance — and "saffron" as a color simply means that same warm golden-yellow.
